newsitem.title: USA: Reno seen resisting special probe U.S. campaigns.
newsitem.headline: Reno seen resisting special probe U.S. campaigns.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno faced a high-pressure deadline for decision in the U.S campaign funding controversy on Monday, apparently ready to defy a Republican clamour for an independent counsel.

Reno has long resisted calls to seek a Watergate-style investigator to probe the fund-raising practices of President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party and White House, saying she had yet to see the sort of specific, credible evidence of wrongdoing the independent counsel law requires.

But she has come under intense pressure -- including threats of retaliation -- to change that stand and do it in writing because of a formal request from Republicans who run the congressional committees with jurisdiction over the issue.
The law sets a 30-day deadline for replying to such requests, which effectively expired on Monday.
A House Judiciary Committee staff member said Reno's letter was not expected until late Monday afternoon -- and the betting around Washington was that it would say "no."
"From everything I have heard, Reno will turn them down," a senior Justice Department official said late last week, a view widely shared and supported by Reno's position to date.
The independent counsel law demands "specific information" from a "credible source" that a covered official has committed a federal crime, a threshold Reno says has not been met.

The law derives from the Watergate scandal of 1972-74 in which then-President Richard Nixon fired Archibald Cox, the first official appointed to investigate the abuse-of-power allegations that eventually drove Nixon from office. Congress later established a system for appointing investigators independent of such influence and beyond retaliation.
The actual choice is made by a special three-judge panel, acting at the attorney general's request.

Many have been chosen over the years including some at Reno's urging. But she has insisted that Justice Department and congressional inquiries already underway are sufficient to probe the 1996 campaign fund-raising questions involving Clinton and his party.

The main questions raised so far concern possible attempts at illegal or improper influence-peddling involving foreign donors, mainly from Asia, as well as U.S. sources in financing the campaign that re-elected Clinton.
Reno's stance has prompted menacing talk from Republicans who intimate they may seek her head.

House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich on Sunday threatened to haul Reno before Congress to testify under oath about her decision and whether it was influenced by the White House unless she calls for an independent probe.

"If she can look at the day-after-day revelations about this administration and not conclude it's time for an independent counsel, how can any serious citizen have any sense of faith in her judgment?" Gingrich asked on the "Fox News Sunday" programme.
He criticised Reno particularly for not ensuring the White House knew of FBI concerns that China was planning illegal contributions to election campaigns last year.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat and a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sprang to Reno's defence on Monday. "The attorney general should have the freedom to call the shots," she told reporters," adding: "There is no one I know who is straighter or more honest than Janet Reno."
If Reno should decide to go along with Republican demands, she then would have to open a preliminary inquiry lasting at least 90 days before deciding to seek an independent counsel.
